To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please read: fake blue pills, and what to do if someone goes down

This is its own post because I don't want it buried. Please read it all the way through, even if your kids are small, even if you think it's nothing to do with you.

Neighbourhood Policing put a warning up on here on Friday and I don't think many people have seen it. Blue tablets are being sold round south Manchester as diazepam or "Xanax". They're fake. Some of them contain nitazenes, which are synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. Whoever takes one has no way of knowing what's in it. It looks like a pill, it's sold like a pill, but it isn't.

Signs someone is in trouble:
- extreme drowsiness, can't be woken properly
- tiny, pinpoint pupils
- slow or noisy breathing
- blue lips

If you see any of that, ring 999 straight away. Not in ten minutes, not after you've tried to walk them round, not after you've asked their mate what they took. Straight away.

What I really need people to hear is this. Please don't put them to bed to sleep it off. It's the most natural thing in the world when your mate is out of it and you're scared. You think they'll be fine in the morning, and you ring someone hours later when it's got worse. By then the brain has been without oxygen too long. Sleeping it off is the thing that kills people. Ring early, even if you feel daft afterwards, even if it turns out to be nothing.

And don't worry about getting in trouble. The police themselves have said their priority is preserving life. That's the actual word from them. Nobody is going to care what you were doing or who brought what. Ring.

Naloxone is a nasal spray that reverses the effects of opioids, and it can buy time. You can get it free from Brightpath drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette. Anyone can ask, and you don't have to give your name. The training takes about 10 minutes. They're open Monday to Friday 10 to 4, and Thursdays till 7. It doesn't replace the 999 call, you still ring, but having it in the house or in a bag could make a real difference.

Now, to the parents, and I'm one too. I had this chat with my own lad (he's 14) last night over his tea. There were eye rolls. He listened though, and he asked me what pinpoint pupils meant, so it went in. Please have the conversation this week. Not after half term, not when there's a better moment, because there isn't one. Keep it short and calm, and tell them the three things: the pills aren't what they say they are, if a mate goes down you ring 999 immediately, and you will never be in trouble with us for ringing.

To the teenagers if you're reading this: I'm a nurse, and I'm not here to lecture you. I just don't want anyone's friend left to sleep it off.

One more thing. I've seen the thread about Saturday, and I'm not going to add to it. Whatever's true, there are families going through the worst thing right now, and the admins have asked us not to guess, so I won't. But I will say this: slagging kids off doesn't help anybody. A scared kid doesn't ring for help, and that is the whole problem. If a young person thinks they'll get a bollocking, or worse, they'll hesitate, and hesitating is what we can't afford. If we want them to ring, they need to know it's safe to.

So please, share this. Don't just like it. Post it on your own page, send it to the parents' WhatsApp, show it to your teenagers, put it on the school group, print it and stick it up at work. The more people who know this, the better the chance that someone does the right thing on the night.

Thanks for reading. Ring 999, don't wait, and talk to your kids this week.

Becky
